claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed primarily by the degree of atomic-scale homogenization achieved during synthesis.
Atomic-scale homogenization minimizes local lattice strain.
Minimizing local lattice strain suppresses defect-mediated phase segregation at service temperatures.
Conventional physical and chemical synthesis routes produce nanoparticles with varying degrees of atomic mixing.
Higher reduction rates or rapid quenching can enhance atomic mixing.
Standard synthesis conditions lead to modest atomic segregation.
Catalytic service regimes typically span 773–1173 K.
Thermoelectric service regimes typically span 473–1923 K.
Enhanced atomic mixing reduces localized strain and the concentration of defect sites.
Localized strain and defect sites can nucleate phase segregation or elemental migration at high temperatures.
Reducing localized strain and defect sites preserves a homogeneous solid-solution structure during high-temperature operation.
Enhanced-mixing nanoparticles will exhibit less phase segregation than the control after high-temperature exposure.
Enhanced-mixing nanoparticles will exhibit less coarsening than the control after high-temperature exposure.
Enhanced-mixing nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than the control after high-temperature exposure.
The standard baseline is expected to have greater localized lattice strain and an earlier onset of phase segregation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when lattice strain caused by elemental mismatch is significant.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to systems with strong intrinsic ordering tendencies.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when external environmental factors such as oxidizing atmospheres dominate stability.
Extended annealing at moderate temperatures enhances local elemental clustering.

contradictions.description: The stated control and baseline use standard synthesis conditions, whereas the falsification experiment replaces that baseline with a deliberately clustering-promoting extended anneal. This changes the comparison and may confound atomic mixing with thermal history.
